identity.title: Exploring The Loss Landscape Of Regularized Neural Networks Via Convex Duality

problem.claim: Analyze stationary points, global-optimum connectivity, non-increasing-loss paths, and nonuniqueness in regularized neural-network loss landscapes.

contributions.claim: Recasts the neural-network landscape problem as an equivalent convex problem and studies its dual.
For scalar-output two-layer networks, characterizes the convex solution set and all stationary points, then identifies width-dependent topology changes and continuum-valued optima.
Extends solution-set and connectivity results to vector-valued two-layer and parallel three-layer architectures.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors' stated approach is to use convex duality to characterize landscape structure and extend the resulting connectivity analysis across architectures.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a phase transition in the topology of global optima as network width changes.
The authors report counterexamples with a continuum of optimal solutions.
The authors report that their characterization and connectivity results extend to two-layer vector-valued and parallel three-layer networks.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames four landscape properties: stationary points, optimal-solution connectivity, non-increasing-loss paths to arbitrary global optima, and nonuniqueness.
It casts the analysis as an equivalent convex problem and examines its dual.
For scalar-output two-layer networks, it characterizes the convex solution set and all stationary points.
It reports width-driven topology phase transitions, continuum-optimum counterexamples, and extensions to several architectures.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a dual characterization of an equivalent convex problem to claims about stationary points, topology, connectivity, and nonuniqueness.

lessons.interpretation: A structural representation can align several landscape claims under one analytical object.
lessons.application: When presenting a theory paper, introduce the representation first, then map each claimed consequence explicitly to the part of the representation that supports it.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed reformulation is not shown to preserve the property being analyzed.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the regularizer, data assumptions, activation functions, width thresholds, or formal definitions of connectivity and phase transition.
It does not provide the conditions or constructions underlying the reported extensions and counterexamples.
